sentences.sentence: Illustration by Fresh Idea
Full manuscript in two months.
That was the goal.
I was on vacation in Mexico, no less, when I checked my email and saw the opportunity.
It was mid-June and the conference was happening near the summer solstice.
The proposal had come in from a publishing house that I had a soft spot for.
We would call it an "emergency proposal".
They had one spot left and would accept a manuscript that was already written or "well underway".
Well underway was the key.
The more I thought about it, the more excited I got.
This was the chance to get published by my number one publisher.
I was going to show them my stuff and I was going to get published.
I had two months to write it.
That was the deadline, and I was determined to hit it.
So I started writing.
I sat down on that first day and wrote 2,000 words.
The next day I wrote 5,000 more.
It was like a dam had burst.
The ideas were flowing, and I was cranking them out.
And then it happened.
I hit a snag.
Not a big one, but a snag.
A few days into writing, I noticed that my writing was not as good as I thought it was.
I was having trouble coming up with the right words.
I was having trouble making the characters sound right.
It was not flowing like it was before.
And then it hit me.
My ego was getting in the way.
I had a vision in my mind of what this book was going to be.
I had a vision of how the story was going to end.
And I was determined to make it happen.
I was determined to make it perfect.
But the more I wrote, the more I realized that it was not working.
I was trying to force it to fit into the mold.
And that's when I realized it.

sentences.sentence: **What in the World is Shaking Up The Hospitality Industry?
How prepared are you for the revolution?
Once upon a time, not that long ago in the restaurant, food and hospitality industry, the formula for success was pretty simple to grasp.
Following the formula was widely accepted as the guaranteed path to making a name for yourself, attracting and retaining customers, and generating revenue.
The formula went something like this: build a beautiful space, train your staff to be attentive and friendly, cook good food, set prices right, and market it well.
If you followed these simple steps, you'd be golden.
The market was relatively straightforward and the rules were easy to follow.
But not anymore.
Things have changed.
The hospitality industry is undergoing a revolution.
Not just any revolution, but a digital and customer-centric driven revolution.
A revolution where the consumer is in control and the restaurant is at their mercy.
A revolution where technology can change a customer's experience in a restaurant with the push of a button.
A customer who used to be just another face in the crowd, now has the power to be heard and the power to share with everyone.
The shift began with the rise of the smartphone and social media.
With just a click, a customer can leave a review about their experience in your restaurant.
They can rate you on Google or Yelp and let all their friends know about it.
They can take a picture of their meal and post it.
This has put the customer in control and has made the restaurant very careful about how they treat their customers.
They have to be perfect or they will be known all over the internet and their customers will be gone.
The next thing that happened was the rise of online ordering and delivery.
With just a click, a customer can order a meal and have it delivered to their door.
This has changed the way a lot of restaurants do business.
They have to have a way to take online orders and have it delivered quickly.

sentences.sentence: **The #1 Thing That Gets Me Through Difficult Days**
My coping mechanism in trying times.
Photo by Ian Chen on Unsplash
I remember the first few hours after my mother took her last breath.
The crushing weight of loss, the empty silence in my home, the overwhelming grief that felt like it was suffocating me.
I also remember the first few days.
The days that felt like an eternity, the days that made me question my purpose, the days that made me question my sanity.
Those were the darkest days of my life.
But, somehow, amidst all that darkness, there was something that kept me going.
Something that still gets me through the difficult days.
That one thing is my journal.
There's something about putting my thoughts down on paper that makes it real.
It makes me face the pain head-on.
It gives me permission to feel.
It's my way of releasing the weight that's inside me.
And, when I sit down to write, it's like taking a deep breath.
It's like letting go of the air that's trapped in my lungs and filling them up again.
It's like coming up for air.
I used to be the type of person who avoided talking about my feelings.
I avoided talking about my emotions.
I avoided talking about my problems.
But, when I started writing in my journal, it all came out.
And, it was like a weight was lifted off my shoulders.
It was like I could finally exhale.
And, that's what I do on the hard days.
I write.
I write until I can't write anymore.
I write until I'm tired.
I write until I'm crying.
And, when I'm done, I feel like I can finally sleep.
Not only does writing help me process my emotions, but it also helps me see things from a different perspective.
It helps me see that I'm not alone.
It helps me see that I'm strong.

Secondly, "The Well" is a great way to engage with others in the community.

It's a great way to engage with others, to share with others, and to learn from others.
It's a great way to grow in community and to grow in your faith.
It's a way to make a deeper connection with others and to know that you are not alone.
Thirdly, "The Well" is a great way to stay on track with your faith.

Dear Reader,
Welcome to my little corner of the world!

* Hope – because even when it’s hard to see, it’s not gone
* Dreams – because they are for the dreaming, the working, and the believing
On this page, you'll find me talking about what's on my heart, on my mind, and in my life.
Some of it might be easy to read, some of it might be hard.

sentences.sentence: **Happy Birthday, Sidra**
I woke up as a different person today.
I am an altogether different person this year.
But I still feel like the 13-year-old me is watching me over.
I remember how she never wanted to grow up, thinking she'd lose the carefree spirit, the spark that danced in her eyes, the innocence that made her heart sing.
But life has a way of surprising you, of changing you in ways you never thought possible.
And yet, I'm still me.
A lot can happen in 13 years – growth, change, love, loss, laughter, and tears.
You get to experience your first kiss, your first heartbreak, your first job, and your first independence.
You get to discover who you are, what you want, and what you need.
You get to find your voice, to speak your truth, and to make your voice heard.
It's a long journey, full of ups and downs, twists and turns, but it's yours alone.
And I'm so proud of you, Sidra, for making it this far.
As you blow out the candles on your birthday cake, remember the little girl who never wanted to grow up.
Remember her spark, her laughter, her tears, and her dreams.
Remember the little girl who was you, and hold onto her.
Don't lose her in the process of becoming someone else.
Don't lose sight of who you are, where you came from, and where you're going.
You're still that same little girl, with the same heart, the same soul, and the same spirit.
Just a little wiser, a little older, and a little more you.
Happy birthday, Sidra.
May all your dreams come true, may you get everything you want, and may you remember to always be you.

sentences.sentence: **"Don't I Know You: A Haunting Portrayal of Lost Innocence in the Shadows of Waikiki's Dancefloors"**
As the fourth and final song faded, the DJ in our club at the north end of Waikiki kept the crowd pumped for another set of nude women on stage under the flashing black lights.
These men were mostly military dudes who were barely legal, teenagers and early twenties, fresh off the mainland with a desire to live large.
They wore their "I'm a player" confidence as a neon sign on their shirt, but behind the bravado, they were lost, searching for more than a good time, for something to make them feel whole.
That's where "Don't I Know You" by Patti Smith, the iconic poet and musician, comes in.
Released in 1975, "Don't I Know You" is a song about a moment in time when everything comes together and you know you have found the one you've been searching for.
The lyrics are a nostalgic look back at the past, to a moment when love was true and real, and the speaker is questioning if she really does know the person who was truly important to her.
But the truth is, that's not what makes the song so haunting, it's not what makes it so real.
It's the desperation, the desperation to belong, to be loved, to be someone.
On that dancefloor in Waikik, the music didn't sound like it should, it sounded like a dream that was slowly fading away.
It was like the beat of the song was pounding in our heads, but the words were like a whisper, a whisper that only we could hear.
We were all lost, we were all searching, we were all thinking about something more.
Something more than the next drink, the next woman, the next high.
Something more than this endless party.

sentences.sentence: Photo by Harry Knight on Unslush
"Card games, now that's a good way to pass the time."
An older woman observes my group of fifteen high school students huddled in circles playing games.
We've just spent a week in the great outdoors, disconnected from the world of Wi-Fi and indulged in a much-needed break from the digital haze that has consumed us for far too long.
Her words are a stark contrast to the usual scenario that plays out when we're back in school - laptops open, faces glued to screens, and fingers typing away as fast as they can.
We've become so accustomed to the instant gratification of the digital world that we forget how to truly enjoy ourselves in real life.
The internet has become a major distraction in our lives and we're at a point where we can't go a minute without checking our phones or scrolling through social media.
We get caught up in the endless cycle of notifications, messages, and likes and it's taking over our lives.
We need to get back to real life and spend less time staring at a screen.
We need to start being more present in the moment and enjoy life for what it is, without the filter of the internet.
Getting off the internet is not just about switching off our phones or closing our laptops, it's about a change in our way of thinking and being.
It's about learning to enjoy life without the need for validation from others and to stop comparing ourselves to everyone else's highlight reel.
It's about being present in the moment and enjoying the beauty of nature, the company of others, and the simplicity of life.
The benefits of getting off the internet are many.
It can help us relax and reduce stress, it can help us be more present and enjoy life, and it can help us think and learn more clearly.
When we're not constantly connected to the internet, we have time to think and think deeply about things.

sentences.sentence: **Simple Changes That Helped Me Lose 5 Kg and Feel Great in Just One Month**
Image by biscoto87
When the pandemic-induced lock-down happened, I lost all motivation.
My life became sedentary.
Up until then, I had maintained a relatively active lifestyle, going for walks and doing some light jogging during my free time.
